name: Executive Function and Behavior Support
title: Executive Function and Behavior Support
answer: Executive function and behavior support means using AI to help students with disabilities plan, organize, and manage time, and to help staff create visual schedules, social narratives, and behavior data charts. It matters because these supports can make school more predictable and help students build their own skills instead of depending on a tool. The decisions about what a student needs and what a pattern means stay with educators and the behavior team.

sections.body: Many students with disabilities have trouble with executive function, which includes planning, organizing, and managing time. AI can take a large assignment and break it into smaller steps with deadlines, which makes the work easier to start and track. Students can use Google Calendar to schedule those steps, and students 13 and older can use Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat through a school account for planning help. The aim is not to have the tool do the work forever but to build the student's own skills over time. Visual schedules and social narratives serve a related purpose by helping students with autism or anxiety know what to expect.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a student might get a big project split into steps, with each step placed on a calendar so the student can see what comes next. For students 13 and older, a school account for Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat can be used to help plan, while calendar scheduling is available to students generally. Teachers can create visual schedules and social narratives quickly with tools such as Boardmaker and Canva for Education. The special education teacher or counselor reviews any narrative written for a specific student, and it should be simple, positive, and true to that student's situation. For behavior plans, staff record when behaviors happen, what came before, and what followed, then AI features in spreadsheets can chart the data and point out patterns, such as clusters at certain times or in certain settings.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no study, figure, or evidence label for this idea. It describes practice and references earlier chapters, Chapter 11 for building student skills and Chapter 5 for visual schedules and social narratives, but it does not report research findings. So this idea rests on practice rather than research as far as the text states.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on what AI should do. The goal is to build the student's own skills over time rather than leave them dependent on the tool. A special education teacher or counselor must review social narratives written for a specific student, and each narrative should be simple, positive, and true to the student's situation. For behavior plans, the behavior team interprets the patterns and decides what to change, because a chart cannot know why a student is struggling. The decisions about support and behavior remain with people, not with the AI.
